summary: Bunker Island (Bug) Light guards the entrance to Yarmouth Harbour. First lit in 1874 on a reef, rebuilt in 1924 and 1959, and automated by 1984; the keepers' families lived at the light.

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property. Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Reached on foot at low tide from a gate on a gravel road; do not climb the tower.

events.note: Work on the reef light; NSLPS gives the began date as 1873
Joshua Doane, first keeper, salary $350 a year
Formal dwelling built on the cribwork
Dwelling moved to a new concrete and steel pier, 36 feet across
North End light, north-west extremity of the island, put in operation 15 January 1907
Collision of the steamer Prince George with the barque Lowwood in Yarmouth harbour, Tuesday 30 July 1907, in fog; the testimony about passing Bunker island light (Bug) comes from this inquiry
Fourth-order dioptric lens, fog bell in operation (NSLPS)
Steam tug John C. Stoneman used temporarily as a lightship; moved to a new position July 1923
Second tower put in operation April 1924; square wood tower on a dwelling, on a red caisson
Fourth-order dioptric lens and mechanical fog bell (NSLPS, second tower)
Present square concrete tower replaced the second tower (NSLPS). The station record's Lighthouse Directory gives 1960.
Last keeper on the NSLPS list, Charles Manser, served to 1981 (the NSLPS dates automation by 1984)
Automated by 1984 (NSLPS); lantern room added to the tower in 1984 (Lighthouse Friends)
Dioptric lens, electric lantern and fog signal in operation (NSLPS)

wrecks.vessel: Cohan (the report's heading spells it Coban)
wrecks.date_note: Printed in the Department's annual report for 1909; the printed passage does not give the date of the grounding
wrecks.outcome: Engines stopped while rounding Bunker Island light; the strong current of the ebbing tide 'nipped her starboard bow', putting her onto the edge of Sallows Rock shoal. The inquiry found the pilot blameworthy for not keeping the ship in the deepest water.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NSLPS dates the present tower to 1959 and says it replaced the second tower. The station record's source, the Lighthouse Directory, gives 1960. Lighthouse Friends says it was erected not long before Jules Cottreau retired in 1963. The story uses 1959 from the NSLPS and notes the 1960 date.
Lighthouse Friends calls the 1874 foundation crib-work, following the Department's description; the NSLPS calls it a caisson. Both are given in the story.
Lighthouse Friends gives 1931 and the NSLPS 1930 as the start of Cottreau's service. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: 1) Keeper dates: NSLPS starts Jules Cottreau in 1930 and lists 'Doane, Mr.' for 1930; Lighthouse Friends gives F. H. Doane 1904 to 1930, B. A. Doane 1930 to 1931, Cottreau 1931 to 1963. Unresolved; the story gives both. 2) Joshua Doane (1874 to 1901) rests on Lighthouse Friends alone; the Department's name indexes for 1900 to 1904 print 'Doane, Joshua' with no station. 3) The 1911 and 1912 keepers' tables print Bunker's Island and North End stations with keepers in a layout that is read by column position (for example F. H. Doane beside 'Bunker's Island' in 1912). Only the 1907 entry, where 'Doane, F. H' and 'Bunker Island' sit together, is used for the roster. Checked 2026-10-28: the 1912 table prints 'Bunker's Island; F. H. Doane' and 'I. North End Jas. H. Schoville' on single lines, which confirms Doane at Bunker's Island in 1912; the 1910 table gives a 1904 appointment for Doane (OCR 'Tidy 27, 1904', read by column position). James H. Schoville (appointed 16 January 1907 per the 1910 table) is not on the roster because the North End light is a separate structure from the 1874 light; the editor should decide whether he belongs to this station's roster. 4) Cohan: the report's heading spells the steamer's name Coban; the text reads Cohan. The printed passage gives no date for the grounding. Checked 2026-10-28: the casualty list (scan 214) and the passage itself (scan 224 to 225) give no date, so it stays undated and out of the events list. 5) Prince George: the collision (Tuesday 30 July 1907, Yarmouth harbour, with the barque Lowwood) is dated in the report at scan 229; the engineer's testimony is at scan 230. The collision is an event in the events list, not a wreck. 6) The Atlantic Advocate (May 1965) quotation reaches us only as Lighthouse Friends prints it; the child is not named and no family member is named beyond the keeper. 7) Present tower: NSLPS 1959; the station record (Lighthouse Directory) 1960; Lighthouse Friends 'not long before' 1963. 8) Stoneman: Lighthouse Friends says the tug marked the station until April 1924; the Department says the tug was moved to a new position in July 1923. Both are in the story. 9) The 1874 construction and the 1941 lens rest on the NSLPS and Lighthouse Friends alone; the corpus has no Department report before 1900 that covers the first light. 10) No Canadian newspaper search run (newspapers.py covers US papers, and a Chronicling America search for Bunker Island and Yarmouth returned no relevant page). 11) The 'Bug Light' name comes from the 1909 report's usage; the station record's Wikipedia and tourism-site mentions were not cited. 12) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the archive.org page images for the 1907 Doane entry (scan 151) and the 1910 table could not be opened from the browser pane (access denied), so the Doane column pairing in 1907 is checked against the OCR and the 1912 line-paired table only. 13) The Cohan date is still unknown; the Prince George collision (30 July 1907) is now dated from the report text at scan 229.
